summary: Signal Delay is a browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players design a robotic mission to the Moon or Mars against four real limits: weight, budget, power and data. They choose the objective, the rocket, the science orbit and the parts that fit the rocket's nose. Then they fly it. The mission runs day by day under the real sky, and every order travels to the spacecraft at the speed of light, so a solar storm can arrive before the command does. At Mars the robot asks what to photograph. Real NASA images come home through Deep Space Network passes, and the science returned is the score. Every number comes from NASA data (JPL ephemerides, NSSDC fact sheets, DSN documents, real mission figures), and players can open each one to see its source. The Daily mission replays last week's real solar storms from NASA DONKI. The report compares the flight with the real NASA mission and suggests one change to try next. The game plays in English and Bangla, solo or as a team of 2–4 on phones.
details:
▎What it does. Signal Delay is a free browser game, playable at https://shariar165.github.io/Signal-Delay/ with nothing to install, that turns the work of a NASA mission team into three steps:

▎ 1. Design (Pack): choose a mission objective, a rocket, a science orbit and parts. Live bars show weight, budget, power and data before you commit. A bigger rocket lifts more but costs more. A high orbit saves fuel and reaches Deimos but makes Phobos expensive.

▎ 2. Fly & Survive: the mission runs day by day. Danger cards (solar storms, dust storms, eclipses, part failures) stop the clock, and your order crosses space at light speed (3–22 minutes to Mars). At Mars the robot asks what to observe. Six real targets each cost fuel, battery or risk, and each picture comes home on a booked DSN pass.

▎ 3. Mission Report: the album of pictures that made it home, the robot's last message, a comic of your flight, a comparison with the real NASA mission, and one concrete change for next time. FLY AGAIN shows how each limit moved.

▎ How it works. A TypeScript engine computes the physics: Lambert transfers between real dates from JPL's planetary elements, rocket-equation Δv, payload versus launch energy, solar power and eclipses day by day, battery sizing, the DSN link budget, and light time. Real missions (MAVEN, LRO/LCROSS, OSIRIS-REx, Mars Climate Orbiter) run through the same model as player designs and are validated against published values. Every constant keeps its source, and players can open it with ⓘ. Anything that is a game estimate is labelled as one.

▎ Live NASA data. "Mars right now" shows today's Earth–Mars distance and light time. The Daily mission replays the last week of NASA DONKI solar energetic particle events and CMEs, using WSA-ENLIL Mars-arrival predictions.

▎ Benefits and impact. It is built for students first (Cadet mode), with Engineer mode showing each equation and input. It teaches that mission design is a chain of trade-offs, and that a team far from its spacecraft must plan ahead. Mars Climate Orbiter's loss is retold as a playable lesson. It plays in English and Bangla, so students in Bangladesh can play in their own language. Team Mode lets 2–4 players share one mission with roles and votes, on one screen or each on their own phone in an online room.

▎ Tools. TypeScript, React 19, Vite, three.js (3D Mars and Moon globes), the Web Audio API, Supabase Realtime (online rooms), Vitest (905 tests) and Playwright, with GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for deploys and the daily DONKI fetch.

▎ What is creative. The delay itself is the game mechanic: you never control the robot directly, you only send it orders that arrive late. The robot talks back on a teletype, pictures print as they come down, and real NASA postcards are earned as rewards.

▎ Factors we considered. Honesty of data (no invented numbers, and estimates are labelled), phone and desktop layouts, reduced motion, accessibility for new players (briefings, a coach, a launch checklist) and a game that runs offline from a static site.
